title: From “brain drain” to “brain gain”: The case for global skill partnerships in healthcare
gist: World Bank economists argue Global Skill Partnerships (GSPs), which finance health-worker training in origin countries and split graduates between 'home' and 'abroad' tracks, can turn the ~15 million global health-worker shortfall into 'brain gain'. Evidence cited: the Philippines-Germany nursing GSP (300+ nurses, ~200 on the home track), nine extra Philippine nurses licensed per US emigrant, and pre-departure credential recognition to avoid 'brain waste'.

themes.theme: Scale of the shortage and the GSP model

insights.claim: The world faces a shortfall of approximately 15 million health workers, while many potential workers in lower-income countries lack competitive training.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Structural healthcare labor shortage sustains demand for cross-border staffing and training.
insights.quote: The world faces a shortfall of approximately 15 million health workers.

insights.claim: Global Skill Partnerships finance training in a worker's home country and place graduates either in domestic jobs (home track) or in legal jobs abroad (abroad track).
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A replicable employer-funded model for workforce pipelines.

themes.theme: Brain drain to brain gain evidence

insights.claim: Under the Philippines-Germany GSP, as of April 2025 more than 300 nurses had been trained or were in training, with almost 200 working or planning to work in the Philippines via the home track.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Home-track design measurably mitigates brain drain.

insights.claim: In the Philippines, migration incentives were associated with nine additional nurses licensed domestically for every nurse who migrated to the United States.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Emigration prospects can expand rather than deplete origin-country skill stocks.
insights.quote: migration incentives were associated with nine additional nurses licensed domestically for every nurse who migrated to the United States

insights.claim: Prospects of working abroad raise expected returns to health education, spurring private-sector investment in training in origin countries.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Private nursing education in sending countries benefits from migration demand.

insights.claim: The German-Kosovar diaspora invested in Heimerer Medical College in Kosovo, where most graduates work domestically.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Diaspora capital can fund origin-country health education.

themes.theme: Reducing brain waste and supporting integration

insights.claim: Early in Germany's Triple Win healthcare mobility program, nurses waited up to two years for full accreditation, working below their qualifications at lower salaries.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Credential recognition delays waste labor value in destination markets.
insights.quote: nurses from sending countries waited up to two years for full accreditation

insights.claim: The GSP model requires language training and credentials to be completed before departure so nurses arrive fully recognized with access to higher salaries and residency pathways.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Pre-departure accreditation improves productivity and retention of migrant health workers.

insights.claim: Canada's recognition of nursing qualifications from Aga Khan University in Pakistan offers another model for GSPs.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Mutual recognition deals open labor corridors.

insights.claim: Nurses on the Philippines-Germany GSP abroad track stay with the same employer despite no employment bond, suggesting advanced language training supports retention.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Upfront language investment lowers employer turnover costs.

insights.claim: Japan's nursing and caregiving programs with Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam include Japanese language training supported by JICA via online portals, mobile apps and consultation services.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Aging Asian economies are building structured care-worker import channels.

insights.claim: The 2026 amendments to the WHO Global Code of Practice on International Recruitment of Health Personnel encourage co-investment in health systems and expand the Code's scope to include care workers.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Regulatory shift legitimizing employer-funded recruitment with origin co-investment.

insights.claim: In the Philippines-Germany GSP, German employers finance training, migration and accreditation costs plus modern equipment, curriculum upgrades and scholarships at partner nursing schools.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Employer financing is a template for private capital in skill systems.

insights.claim: World Bank aged-care GSPs link Colombia, Ecuador and Dominican Republic with Spain, and Kenya with Canada, co-investing in origin-country healthcare training.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Aged-care demand in rich aging countries is driving new labor corridors.

insights.claim: GSPs must respond to origin countries' health and employment priorities to build political support.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Political acceptability in sending countries is the gating factor for scale.
insights.quote: GSPs must respond to origin countries’ health and employment priorities to build political support.

insights.claim: South-South and intra-regional GSPs, such as aged care from Solomon Islands to Niue and nursing from Papua New Guinea to Fiji, are growing in importance given the shortage's scale; South Asia offers similar opportunities as Sri Lanka's working-age population peaks.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Health labor mobility is diversifying beyond South-North corridors.
insights.locator: 5. South-South and intra-regional GSPs are growing.

insights.claim: The World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and bilateral donors including the Belgian Development Agency are paying increasing attention to the GSP model.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Rising multilateral funding interest for skills-mobility programs.
insights.locator: 5. South-South and intra-regional GSPs are growing.
